why: With leverage near 1 a random matched-norm difference moves the cued base as much as RL's delta does, so it recovers most of the 410-to-463 gain, as the random edit did on Qwen.
Recovering most of the gain means fixing most of the 65 problems RL fixes among the base's 90 wrong ones, offset by about 15 new losses, giving about 52 fixes.
A generic perturbation of this norm shifts the base toward RL's longer, finished answers, so mean tokens move from the base's 3,933 most of the way to RL's 4,694.
The dose curve saturates early because the magnitude head acts at small scale, so a quarter dose already gives most of the 410-to-463 gain.
At half dose the saturating curve is near its plateau, close to RL's 463.
The curve peaks before a = 1, as the bytegraft curve does at 0.7-0.8, so a = 0.75 sits at or slightly above RL's level.
Past a = 1.1 the delta leaves its working range and the model collapses like the bytegraft dose curve, losing a large share of even the base's 410.
The collapse at a = 1.5 shows up as degenerate text, so a large minority of answers end in word salad.
Without the cue the saturating curve still delivers most of the plain base's 224-to-463 gain at a quarter dose.
At half dose the plain-prompt curve is near its plateau just below RL's 463.
Half dose reaches about 458, which with about 12 losses (RL's base-only count) means about 60 of the base's 90 wrong problems fixed.
Math-RL and Code-RL share the update mask and the function sits in where and how much weights move, not in signs, so Code-RL with the cue lands near Math-RL's level.
With function shared through the update mask, Code-RL carries most of the math gain without the cue too, landing a little below Math-RL's plain 463.
The function sits in large entries and high-magnitude units, so the always-on outlier neurons close far more than their 0.13 % share, about twice the best 0.1 % attribution set's 5.4 % on T1 text.
Same magnitude-concentration argument on RL text, scaled by the usual T2/T1 ratio of about 1.35 in the transplant curves.
